The stellar production — which sees many of its cast, including its two leads, making their Broadway debut — succeeds in threading the needle between two nearly impossible tasks that come with putting on Romeo + Juliet.

Gold’s last two excursions with Shakespeare on Broadway did not fare so well despite “King Lear” starring Glenda Jackson and “Macbeth” starring Daniel Craig. Far more memorable were his revelatory productions of “Hamlet” with Oscar Isaac at the Public Theater and “Othello” with Craig and David Oeylowoh at the New York Theater Workshop.
Even when Connor’s Romeo and Zegler’s Juliet square off from opposite sides of the venue, their invisible chains – hormones, by another term – are magic.
The cast’s relative lack of stage experience is manifest in a flattening of both the poetry and the tragedy.
With its energetic and game cast, Romeo + Juliet on Broadway is enjoyable, but uneven.

Gold tries his damnedest to bring something new to William Shakespeare’s 1597 play, which has been performed in just about every space imaginable for the last four centuries, including three dozen times on Broadway. He occasionally achieves something gorgeous and intimate, thanks in large part to the white-hot chemistry of his two leads.

The most gorgeous moments in this Romeo + Juliet are the simplest, when all the noise falls away and it’s just Connor and Zegler: their first meeting, when they spontaneously proclaim their love in a shared 14-line sonnet; the famous Act 2 balcony scene, a positively swoon-worthy moment that no future production should ever attempt to re-create;...
The entire production flagrantly panders to them, so perhaps they’ll appreciate it more than older folks.
Gold bombards the audience with a reworking short on poetry and long on physical and vocal horseplay.
A new production, one like you’ve likely never seen, with standout performances and a fabulous and aligned design team, Romeo + Juliet defies the stars and brings magic to Circle in the Square.
Zegler's Juliet is an absolute tour de force masterpiece.
In every aspect, Connor delivers one of the most impressive Broadway debuts in many years.
It's a phenomenal display of world building methods that wash over the audience with lavish sensory detail.
Those theatergoers unencumbered by memories of other productions of Romeo and Juliet may more easily embrace this post-modern take on Shakespeare's tragedy.
While Connor and Zegler are passionate as Romeo and Juliet, they display little chemistry when together.
It's hard to escape the feeling that the audience, regardless of age, is being patronized.
What’s more problematic is that Gold doesn’t appear to have any unifying approach to the play aside from creating moments that might play well on TikTok or Instagram Reels.
